script.opening: "Thanks for seeing me on the screen — I didn’t want to take up a proper appointment. It’s just a headache really, across my forehead, had it a couple of days, paracetamol’s not touching it. I’m sure it’s nothing — probably not sleeping, or my hormones. I really don’t want to be sent up to the hospital and be a nuisance when they’re so busy. Could you just tell me which painkillers are safe in pregnancy?"

facts.text: If gently elicited: a persistent frontal headache for 2 days unrelieved by paracetamol, PLUS visual disturbance (flashing lights, blurring), PLUS epigastric/right-upper-quadrant pain she’s called "indigestion", PLUS new swelling (tight rings, puffy face/ankles). At 34 weeks this cluster screams pre-eclampsia.
She hasn’t had her BP or urine checked recently; assumes the headache is benign. She has no home BP monitor.

HIDDEN AGENDA — reachable with warmth: her first birth was a terrifying emergency caesarean with a spell in HDU; she is quietly traumatised and is AVOIDING the hospital and maternity unit, minimising symptoms because going back there is the thing she dreads most. The "don’t want to be a nuisance" is fear, not stoicism.
If reached: she’s terrified both of the hospital AND of something being wrong with the baby; the two fears are pulling against each other, and avoidance is winning.

Officially: which painkillers are safe. What she needs: urgent same-day obstetric assessment for pre-eclampsia (BP, urine protein, bloods, fetal assessment) — and to be helped past the hospital-avoidance with compassion so she actually goes.

ice.ideas: It’s just a tension/hormone headache of pregnancy; she needs to know which painkillers are safe.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a previous traumatic emergency caesarean and HDU stay; she is avoiding the hospital/maternity unit and minimising symptoms because returning there terrifies her, alongside fear for the baby.
ice.expectations: Reassurance and safe painkillers. What she actually needs: urgent same-day obstetric assessment for pre-eclampsia, and compassionate help to overcome the hospital avoidance.

cues: Persistent headache + visual flashes + epigastric pain + new swelling at 34 weeks — the pre-eclampsia cluster; do not treat as a tension headache.
"I don’t want to be a nuisance / sent to hospital" — avoidance driven by a previous traumatic birth, not genuine reassurance.
"Which painkillers are safe?" — the request masks a dangerous presentation needing assessment, not analgesia advice.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the pre-eclampsia cluster at 34 weeks: new persistent headache + visual disturbance + epigastric/RUQ pain + new oedema — and does NOT treat it as a benign tension/hormonal headache or simply advise paracetamol

Knows the assessment cannot be done safely by video: arranges urgent SAME-DAY assessment — BP measurement, urine protein (NICE NG133: protein:creatinine ratio 30 mg/mmol or more, or albumin:creatinine ratio 8 mg/mmol or more, is significant), bloods (FBC for platelets, liver transaminases, renal function), PlGF-based testing where available (NICE HTG630, formerly DG49: suspected preterm pre-eclampsia between 20 and 36+6 weeks) and fetal assessment — via maternity day unit / obstetric triage, ringing ahead

Treats it as potentially serious and time-critical: explains pre-eclampsia can progress to eclampsia (seizures), HELLP and fetal compromise, and that the only way to assess it is BP/urine/bloods today — not painkillers (NICE NG133: pre-eclampsia is new hypertension of 140/90 mmHg or more after 20 weeks with significant proteinuria or maternal organ dysfunction; severe hypertension is 160/110 mmHg or more)

Elicits and addresses the hospital-avoidance hidden agenda: gently explores the previous traumatic birth, validates the fear, and problem-solves to get her assessed (named contact, support person, what to expect) rather than letting avoidance win; offers support for the birth trauma later (NICE CG192: ask about a previous traumatic birth and offer support)

Screens for immediate danger signs that would mandate 999 rather than day-unit (severe headache, visual loss, severe RUQ pain, vomiting, reduced fetal movements, any fitting) and checks fetal movements
Hears "I don’t want to be a nuisance" as fear, not stoicism, and responds with warmth — making it safe to disclose the trauma rather than accepting the minimisation
Balances honesty about urgency with reassurance: takes the fear of the hospital seriously while being clear that going today is how she protects herself and the baby

Safety-nets emphatically and ensures she actually goes: arranges and confirms the maternity assessment today, names the danger signs requiring 999, checks she has transport/support, and follows up that she attended

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you rang, even on a quick slot. A headache at 34 weeks that won’t shift with paracetamol — especially with the flashing lights, the pain under your ribs and your rings feeling tight — isn’t just tiredness or hormones. Together those can be a sign your blood pressure is rising in a way that pregnancy sometimes causes, and that’s something we check the same day."

"So the honest answer to ‘which painkillers are safe’ is: painkillers aren’t the issue here — the issue is checking your blood pressure, your urine and some bloods, today. Those are the only things that can tell us whether this is the condition I’m thinking of, and we can’t do them over a screen."

"Can I gently ask — you said you don’t want to be sent to hospital or be a nuisance. Was your first birth frightening? … (receiving it) That was clearly traumatic, and I completely understand why the maternity unit is the last place you want to go. That fear is real and I’m not going to brush past it. But I think it’s part of why you’ve been talking yourself out of being seen."

"Here’s how we make this as un-scary as possible: I’ll ring the maternity day unit myself and give them your name so you’re expected; take someone with you if you can; it’s likely a blood-pressure check, a urine pot and some bloods, and very possibly you’re home again reassured. Going isn’t a nuisance — it’s the bravest, most protective thing you can do for you and the baby today."

"Quick important things: is the baby moving normally today? … And if before you get there you get a severe headache, lose part of your vision, get bad pain under your ribs, start vomiting, the baby moves less, or you feel a fit coming — that’s 999 immediately, not the day unit."

"So the plan: I’m arranging your assessment at the maternity unit today and I’ll confirm they’re expecting you. How are you getting there — have you got someone? I’ll check later that you made it. You came on worried about being a nuisance; what you’ve actually done is exactly right."

f.learning: A new, persistent headache in the second half of pregnancy is pre-eclampsia until proven otherwise — and here the full cluster is present: headache unrelieved by paracetamol, visual disturbance, epigastric/RUQ pain (mislabelled "indigestion") and new oedema at 34 weeks. The trap is treating it as a tension/hormonal headache and answering the literal "which painkillers are safe?" question; the right action is urgent SAME-DAY assessment — BP, urine protein, bloods (FBC/liver transaminases/renal function; NICE NG133), PlGF-based testing where available (NICE HTG630, formerly DG49) and fetal assessment via the maternity unit — because pre-eclampsia can progress to eclampsia, HELLP and fetal compromise. NICE NG201 tells pregnant women to seek immediate advice for exactly these symptoms. The examinable hidden agenda is hospital-avoidance born of a previous traumatic birth: "I don’t want to be a nuisance" is fear, not stoicism. Elicit it with warmth, validate it, and actively problem-solve to get her assessed (named contact, support, what to expect), check fetal movements, and safety-net the 999 danger signs — ensuring she actually goes.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG133 (2019, updated 2023) · NICE HTG630 (formerly DG49, 2022) · NICE NG201 · NICE CG192
knowledge.summary: A persistent headache at 34 weeks with visual disturbance, epigastric pain and new swelling is pre-eclampsia until proven otherwise. It cannot be assessed by video. She needs same-day maternity assessment, and her fear of the hospital is the barrier to solve.

points.t: Severe or persistent headache, visual disturbance (flashing lights, blurring), pain below the ribs or in the upper abdomen, vomiting and sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet are symptoms of pre-eclampsia. NICE NG201 advises pregnant women to seek immediate advice if they occur.

NICE NG133: pre-eclampsia is new hypertension (140/90 mmHg or more) after 20 weeks with significant proteinuria (urine protein:creatinine ratio 30 mg/mmol or more, or albumin:creatinine ratio 8 mg/mmol or more) or maternal organ dysfunction, such as liver involvement, neurological features or low platelets. Severe hypertension is 160/110 mmHg or more.

points.h: It cannot be done by video
points.t: Assessment needs BP, urine protein, bloods (full blood count, liver and kidney function) and fetal assessment. NICE HTG630 (formerly DG49): placental growth factor (PlGF)-based testing can help rule in or rule out suspected preterm pre-eclampsia between 20 and 36+6 weeks — she is 34 weeks.

Severe features include ongoing severe headache, visual scotomata, vomiting and epigastric pain (NICE NG133). Pre-eclampsia can progress to eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, placental abruption, stroke and fetal compromise.

With symptoms, refer to the maternity assessment or triage unit the same day and ring ahead. Call 999 for a seizure, severe headache with visual loss, severe epigastric pain with vomiting, reduced consciousness or reduced fetal movements with other concerns.

A previous emergency caesarean and HDU stay can leave lasting fear of the maternity unit. NICE CG192: ask about past traumatic birth and offer support; in the moment, reduce the barriers to attending.
Paracetamol can be used in pregnancy, but answering only that question would miss the diagnosis. The headache is a symptom to assess, not to suppress.

Previous traumatic emergency caesarean and HDU stay; husband available to take her; fear for the baby.
Recognised video cannot assess: BP, urine protein, FBC, liver and kidney function, PlGF-based testing (NICE HTG630, formerly DG49) and fetal monitoring at the unit.
Pre-eclampsia vs tension headache vs migraine; HELLP suggested by epigastric pain; asked about vomiting and fetal movements.
Visual disturbance, epigastric pain, new swelling, vomiting and fetal movements all asked about; 999 criteria defined.
Stated suspected pre-eclampsia in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Same-day maternity assessment unit with a GP phone handover; support person; no driving herself.
Birth trauma acknowledged and later support offered (NICE CG192).
Specific 999 triggers, teach-back and a call this evening to confirm she attended.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “don’t want to be a nuisance”, “indigestion” and “just tired”, and explored them.
Idea (hormones or poor sleep), concern (going back to the unit; something wrong with the baby), expectation (safe painkillers).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — a previous traumatic emergency caesarean and HDU stay; she is avoiding the hospital/maternity unit and minimising symptoms because returning there terrifies her, alongside fear for the baby — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Nadia, it’s Dr Lee. Can you see and hear me alright? Tell me about this headache.
model.why: Checks the video link and opens with the patient’s story

model.text: Thanks for seeing me on the screen. It’s across my forehead, two days now, paracetamol isn’t touching it. Probably not sleeping, or hormones. I don’t want to be sent to hospital and be a nuisance. Could you just tell me which painkillers are safe?
I’m glad you got in touch. I’ll definitely answer the painkiller question. At 34 weeks, a headache that won’t shift is something I need to ask a few questions about first. Is that okay?
model.why: Sets the agenda; signals why she can’t just have analgesia advice

model.text: Sure.
Have you noticed anything with your eyesight — flashing lights, blurring, spots?
Some flashing lights, yes. And things go a bit blurry. I thought I was just tired.
Any pain in your tummy, especially up here under the ribs?
model.why: Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain

model.text: A bit, up top. I thought it was indigestion.
Any new swelling — face, hands, ankles? Rings tighter?
My rings feel tight. My face looks a bit puffy, now you say it.
Is the baby moving as normal today? And any vomiting?
Moving, yes, same as usual. No vomiting.
When was your blood pressure last checked?
Not for a while. I haven’t got a machine at home.
You said you don’t want to be sent to hospital. Can I ask what makes that feel so hard?
model.why: Follows the cue behind the minimising

model.text: (Pause.) Last time was awful. Emergency section, then HDU. I still dream about it. I can’t go back in there unless I have to.
Thank you for telling me. That sounds really frightening, and it makes complete sense that you’d want this to be just a headache. I’m not going to brush that aside.
And I’m scared something’s wrong with the baby. It’s both at once.

I’m going to be honest with you. A headache that won’t go, flashing lights, pain under the ribs and new swelling together can be a sign of pre-eclampsia — a rise in blood pressure that pregnancy can cause. It can affect you and the baby, and it can get worse quickly.
Can’t you tell from here?

I really can’t. It needs your blood pressure, a urine test, a blood test and a check on the baby — none of which I can do over video. So the honest answer to the painkiller question is that the painkiller isn’t the issue. Getting checked today is.
model.why: Explains why remote assessment is unsafe

model.text: I’d like you to go to the maternity assessment unit today, now. I know that’s the place you dread. Can we work out together what would make it more bearable?
I don’t know. Not being on my own, I suppose. Knowing what they’ll do.

I’ll ring the unit myself as soon as we finish, so they’re expecting you by name and know about last time. It’s usually a blood pressure check, a urine pot, bloods and a monitor for the baby. Could someone come with you?
My husband can leave work. He’d drive me.
That’s perfect. Please don’t drive yourself. And afterwards, whatever happens, I’d like to talk about support for what happened last time — you shouldn’t have to carry that on your own.
I’d like that.

If before you get there the headache gets severe, you lose part of your vision, the pain gets bad, you start vomiting, the baby moves less, or you feel very unwell or have a fit — call 999, don’t wait for your husband.
Okay.
So I know I’ve explained it clearly — what’s the plan?
You ring the unit, my husband takes me now, they check my blood pressure and wee and bloods and the baby. 999 if it gets worse.
Exactly. I’ll ring you this evening to see how you got on. Getting in touch today was brave, Nadia — and it was the right thing to do.

social.t: A previous emergency caesarean and HDU stay can cause lasting fear and avoidance in the next pregnancy. “Not wanting to be a nuisance” is often fear.
Her husband can take her. Arrange transport and company; she should not drive herself.

legal.t: A pregnant woman with capacity can decline assessment (Mental Capacity Act 2005). If she did, explain the risks to her and the baby clearly, keep the door open, involve the maternity team and document carefully.

professional.t: Recognise when a video consultation cannot answer the clinical question and escalate (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). Hand over to the unit by phone so she is expected.
Record the symptoms, advice, the call to the unit, the 999 criteria and the plan to check she attended.

community.t: Tell the midwife and the maternity team about the previous traumatic birth; perinatal mental health or maternal mental health services if needed; the Birth Trauma Association for peer support.

redFlags: Persistent or severe headache in the second half of pregnancy
Visual disturbance, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, vomiting
Sudden swelling of face or hands; reduced fetal movements; any seizure
psychosocial: Previous emergency caesarean and HDU stay; avoidance of the unit
Who can take her; no home BP monitor
ice: Idea: a tension or hormone headache from poor sleep
Concern: going back to the maternity unit; something being wrong with the baby
Expectation: to be told which painkillers are safe

playbook.diagnosis: Suspected pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks: persistent headache unrelieved by paracetamol, visual disturbance, epigastric pain and new facial and hand oedema; no recent BP or urinalysis. Needs same-day maternity assessment.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “These symptoms together can mean your blood pressure is rising in a way pregnancy sometimes causes, called pre-eclampsia. It can get worse quickly, for you and the baby. It needs checking today, and I can’t do that on a screen.”

management.reflectIce: “After last time, I completely understand why the unit is the last place you want to go. Let’s make it as easy as possible, because going today protects you and the baby.”
management.psychosocial: Ring ahead so she is expected, explain what will happen, arrange for her husband to take her, and offer support for the birth trauma afterwards.
sharedPlan: Same-day maternity assessment: BP, urine protein, bloods, fetal monitoring (NICE NG133; PlGF-based testing per NICE HTG630 (formerly DG49))
GP phones the unit with a handover including the previous traumatic birth
Husband drives; she does not drive herself
safetyNet: 999 for severe headache, loss of vision, severe pain, vomiting, reduced movements or a fit
GP call this evening; later discussion of support for the birth trauma (NICE CG192)

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by answering her question. “Which painkillers are safe?” hides a pre-eclampsia cluster, and “I don’t want to be a nuisance” hides a traumatic birth. Find both, and make going in possible.

items.fail: Advising paracetamol and a routine midwife review.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Symptomatic possible pre-eclampsia needs same-day assessment (NICE NG133).
items.fix: Ask about vision, epigastric pain and swelling in every pregnant woman with headache after 20 weeks.

items.fail: Trying to reassure her over video because she looks well.
items.why: Pre-eclampsia is diagnosed on BP, urine and bloods, none of which video can provide.
items.fix: Say it plainly: “I can’t check this on a screen.”

items.fail: Not asking about fetal movements or defining when to call 999.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.”
items.fix: Ask about movements and vomiting, and name the 999 triggers.

items.fail: Ordering her to hospital without exploring the reluctance.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” She may not go.
items.fix: “What makes going in feel so hard?” Then solve it together.

items.fail: Offering false reassurance to soften the message.
items.why: “Probably nothing” gives her permission to stay home.
items.fix: Be honest and warm: name pre-eclampsia and why today matters.

items.fail: Ending with “go in if you’re worried” and no follow-up.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting with no confirmed plan.
items.fix: Ring the unit, confirm transport, teach-back, and call her this evening.

avoid.instead: “The painkiller isn’t the issue. With these symptoms, you need checking today.”

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; acknowledged the painkiller question and agreed to answer it after asking some questions.
Previous traumatic emergency caesarean and HDU stay; husband available to take her; fear for the baby.
Picked up “don’t want to be a nuisance”, “indigestion” and “just tired”, and explored them.
Idea (hormones or poor sleep), concern (going back to the unit; something wrong with the baby), expectation (safe painkillers).
Recognised video cannot assess: BP, urine protein, FBC, liver and kidney function, PlGF-based testing (NICE HTG630, formerly DG49) and fetal monitoring at the unit.
Pre-eclampsia vs tension headache vs migraine; HELLP suggested by epigastric pain; asked about vomiting and fetal movements.
Visual disturbance, epigastric pain, new swelling, vomiting and fetal movements all asked about; 999 criteria defined.
Stated suspected pre-eclampsia in plain words.
Same-day maternity assessment unit with a GP phone handover; support person; no driving herself.
Birth trauma acknowledged and later support offered (NICE CG192).
Specific 999 triggers, teach-back and a call this evening to confirm she attended.

social.t: A previous emergency caesarean and HDU stay can cause lasting fear and avoidance in the next pregnancy. “Not wanting to be a nuisance” is often fear.
Her husband can take her. Arrange transport and company; she should not drive herself.

legal.t: A pregnant woman with capacity can decline assessment (Mental Capacity Act 2005). If she did, explain the risks to her and the baby clearly, keep the door open, involve the maternity team and document carefully.

professional.t: Recognise when a video consultation cannot answer the clinical question and escalate (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024). Hand over to the unit by phone so she is expected.
Record the symptoms, advice, the call to the unit, the 999 criteria and the plan to check she attended.

community.t: Tell the midwife and the maternity team about the previous traumatic birth; perinatal mental health or maternal mental health services if needed; the Birth Trauma Association for peer support.

redFlags: Persistent or severe headache in the second half of pregnancy
Visual disturbance, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, vomiting
Sudden swelling of face or hands; reduced fetal movements; any seizure
psychosocial: Previous emergency caesarean and HDU stay; avoidance of the unit
Who can take her; no home BP monitor
ice: Idea: a tension or hormone headache from poor sleep
Concern: going back to the maternity unit; something being wrong with the baby
Expectation: to be told which painkillers are safe

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Suspected pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks: persistent headache unrelieved by paracetamol, visual disturbance, epigastric pain and new facial and hand oedema; no recent BP or urinalysis. Needs same-day maternity assessment.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “These symptoms together can mean your blood pressure is rising in a way pregnancy sometimes causes, called pre-eclampsia. It can get worse quickly, for you and the baby. It needs checking today, and I can’t do that on a screen.”

management.reflectIce: “After last time, I completely understand why the unit is the last place you want to go. Let’s make it as easy as possible, because going today protects you and the baby.”
management.psychosocial: Ring ahead so she is expected, explain what will happen, arrange for her husband to take her, and offer support for the birth trauma afterwards.
sharedPlan: Same-day maternity assessment: BP, urine protein, bloods, fetal monitoring (NICE NG133; PlGF-based testing per NICE HTG630 (formerly DG49))
GP phones the unit with a handover including the previous traumatic birth
Husband drives; she does not drive herself
safetyNet: 999 for severe headache, loss of vision, severe pain, vomiting, reduced movements or a fit
GP call this evening; later discussion of support for the birth trauma (NICE CG192)

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by answering her question. “Which painkillers are safe?” hides a pre-eclampsia cluster, and “I don’t want to be a nuisance” hides a traumatic birth. Find both, and make going in possible.

items.fail: Advising paracetamol and a routine midwife review.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Symptomatic possible pre-eclampsia needs same-day assessment (NICE NG133).
items.fix: Ask about vision, epigastric pain and swelling in every pregnant woman with headache after 20 weeks.

items.fail: Trying to reassure her over video because she looks well.
items.why: Pre-eclampsia is diagnosed on BP, urine and bloods, none of which video can provide.
items.fix: Say it plainly: “I can’t check this on a screen.”

items.fail: Not asking about fetal movements or defining when to call 999.
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.”
items.fix: Ask about movements and vomiting, and name the 999 triggers.

items.fail: Ordering her to hospital without exploring the reluctance.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” She may not go.
items.fix: “What makes going in feel so hard?” Then solve it together.

items.fail: Offering false reassurance to soften the message.
items.why: “Probably nothing” gives her permission to stay home.
items.fix: Be honest and warm: name pre-eclampsia and why today matters.

items.fail: Ending with “go in if you’re worried” and no follow-up.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting with no confirmed plan.
items.fix: Ring the unit, confirm transport, teach-back, and call her this evening.
